1.ruledOutBy: We wipe and reinstall everything on it.
1.why: The wipe warning is volunteered precisely so the owner must respond to it; only D acknowledges it. C accepts the overnight loan but is silent on the one thing the technician flagged, so it is a partial-response distractor rather than a rival answer.

2.why: The stimulus is a yes/no confirmation of what the student reported to a colleague. A confirms by echoing the description; C ('Right, I filled that form in with him yesterday') confirms the same report and adds where it was recorded. Nothing in the utterance makes the form-filling claim wrong or off-topic, so C is a fully cooperative confirmation too.

3.why: 'want me to wait while you eat?' is a bare offer with no cue about how far along the diner is or whether waiting is a burden. C accepts, A declines ('I'll box mine up') — both are exactly the replies a competent speaker gives to an offer, and the stimulus supplies nothing to prefer one.

4.why: Only D answers the yes/no question that was actually asked. C (buy the code online) and A (discount) are remedies offered without ever saying whether another copy exists, which is what was requested.

5.why: The definite reference 'the third form' already identifies the outstanding item as shared knowledge, so B's 'Which one are you still waiting on?' asks for information the utterance has just supplied. C and D both proceed as if the key were already available.

6.why: Staff can legitimately answer a fault report either by fixing it (D — a loose safety key is the standard cause of a treadmill cutting out) or by rerouting the user (A — 'the mirror row's free'). The stimulus names both the fault and the location, so each option engages a real part of it and neither is excluded.

7.why: A 4:40 departure with a forty-minute ride arrives at 5:20, so C's acceptance and A's '5:10' are both arithmetically impossible; only B (the 4:10) reaches a five o'clock commitment. Genuinely hard because the stimulus is elliptical and the arithmetic must be done live.

8.why: B notices the mismatch and extends past the presentation, which is the more helpful move — but D simply grants the renewal the student explicitly asked for. The twenty-second is offered as the reason for renewing, not as a request to extend beyond the twentieth, so nothing makes granting the stated request wrong.

9.why: A is the designed answer: Priya holds the file, so the addressee cannot edit it (which does cleanly kill D). But C asserts the name is already on the version Priya has had since Monday, i.e. that the request is moot — a responsive reply that nothing in the stimulus contradicts, since the asker has not seen the deck. This is the weakest of the flags but I can quote nothing that excludes C.

10.ruledOutBy: So it's one more semester of coursework
10.why: 'So it's...' marks a recap of an agreed plan and invites confirmation, which only C gives. D ('if you think that's the smarter route') recasts the recap as a fresh recommendation, and B asks about a term the utterance already specified.

11.ruledOutBy: twelve hours for you this week — two fives and a four?
11.why: Five plus five plus four is fourteen, so D's agreement endorses a total the stimulus itself refutes. C is an aside that leaves the arithmetic unanswered.

12.why: The departure date is withheld, which is what makes C's clarifying question the intended key. But the utterance never says the responder does not know the travel date, and A ('I'll email it Sunday night after I finish the last section') is an ordinary compliant commitment — only B's 'sometime next week' is genuinely unsafe.

13.why: A works the arithmetic (ten-fifty to eleven leaves ten minutes) and is presumably the key, but D refuses the same request for a different, equally ordinary front-desk reason. Nothing in the stimulus establishes an empty waiting room, and staff routinely know queue facts the asker does not; C is also a stock reception reply.

14.ruledOutBy: with the third trial running till ten
14.why: B ('pull the third trial's numbers now') and C ('all three trials plotted by eight') both claim data that does not exist until ten. A promises a final draft sent tonight without accounting for that data arriving at ten, so only D sequences the work around the constraint the speaker raised.

15.ruledOutBy: The instructor has to approve it.
15.why: The third-person 'the instructor' shows the addressee is not the instructor, which kills B. A is the closer competitor — a staffer offering to route the form — but the student has just stated that approval must come from the instructor personally, and A neither signs nor names who will, so it stays a weaker option rather than a rival.

16.why: Twelve hundred over three is four hundred, so D, A and B all accept a figure the stimulus refutes. Minor authoring wobble: the key says 'four each' where it means 'four hundred each'.
